chapter_theme: The last verses of the Namakal Ilampakam: the teacher finishes the story of Civakan's birth, tells the youth it is his own, checks his rage against Kattiyankaran with a promise of a year's restraint, and then tells his own story, a Vidyadhara king turned ascetic whose penance was broken by the elephant-fire hunger and who was cured when the boy fed him; he asks leave to renounce again and departs to wear down his old deeds.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised by Kantukkatan
Civakan's teacher, once the Vidyadhara king Lokamapalan (உலோகமா பாலன், 395); called அருந் தவன், புலவன் and விஞ்சையர் வேந்தன் here; the name Accanandi is traditional and not in these verses
the merchant who takes up and raises the newborn Civakan
the deity who stands by Vijayai when Civakan is born, here blessing the infant
the women who serve food in Kantukkatan's house

386.reading: Continuing the account of Civakan's birth, the teacher tells how the grieving queen went into a forest hard to enter, bore a shining son as a right-whorled conch bears a priceless gem, laid him on a bed of flowers and commended him to good dharma.
386.event: In the teacher's account, Vijayai gives birth in the forest, sets the infant on a flower bed and leaves him with the words நல் அறம் காக்க.
386.nuance: The teacher's version says only புகற்கு அருங் காடு, a forest hard to enter, where the patikam (9) names the burning ground; the mother's last act is to hand the child to aram rather than to any person.

387.reading: The child lying in the forest is likened to the young crescent slipped from the sky and lying amid clustering stars; the lord of the sea-girt earth appeared shining doubly with the gem left beside him, born under the star Uttirattathi, of fame without flaw.
387.nuance: தானத்து மணியும் தானும் இரட்டுறத் தோன்றினானே is taken as the infant and a gem set by him shining together; which gem is meant is not stated in the verse. The naming of the birth star prepares the horoscope praise of 404.

388.reading: As the great ascetic had foretold, the merchant with the garlanded spear went and gladly took up the boy; as he left the child sneezed and a deity spoke a blessing, and the merchant, saying 'listen, my precious one', gave him to his wife, who took him with a love as wide as the sea.
388.event: Kantukkatan takes the infant from the forest as an ascetic had foretold, a deity blesses the child's sneeze, and his wife receives him.
388.nuance: The sneeze answered by a blessing is the household custom of saying 'live long' at a sneeze, here spoken by a deity, so the foundling's first welcome comes from heaven. Whether this is the same deity who stood by Vijayai in the patikam (10) is not said; the one addressed as அரும் பொனாய் is taken to be the merchant's wife.

389.reading: As Krishna once revealed to Karna his birth, the teacher, asked who that great one was, answered 'you', and at the word Civakan's garland, ornaments, chain and earrings slipped, his flower chaplet scattered, and he reeled, lost his senses and fell.
389.event: The teacher tells Civakan that the child of the story is himself, and Civakan faints.
389.nuance: The simile (கரியவன் கன்னற்கு) brings in the Mahabharata scene where Karna learns his royal birth from Krishna: a foundling raised by a lowlier house who learns he is a king's son, the comparison hinting at the claim to a throne that the news now lays on Civakan.

390.reading: The youth fell like a shaken wish-granting tree; the teacher, skilled in speech, quickly went to him, embraced him and consoled him with many good words till he recovered, but the strong-shouldered prince then sank into a sea of grief.
390.event: The teacher revives the fainting Civakan, who wakes into grief.

391.reading: The teacher wipes Civakan's long eyes and tells him that what has befallen him is the sin of such as himself, that he must not brood, nor lament like jewelled women while his enemy still stands, and must put all these thoughts away; and the noble one is comforted.
391.event: The teacher dries Civakan's tears and turns his grief toward the enemy who still lives.

claims.claim: a misfortune that befalls one is the fruit of sin committed
lament befits women, not a man whose enemy lives

391.nuance: எம்மனோர் செய்த பாவம் can mean the sin of people like the speaker or, more loosely, a sin done by 'us', that is by those bound up in the story; either way the teacher names sin, not only Kattiyankaran, as the cause. The consolation does two things at once: it gives karma as the cause and then points to the living enemy, and the second half rouses the anger the next verses must check. The remark that lament is for women is the speaker's, reported as the epic gives it.

392.reading: Roaring like a mountain-splitting lion, raging like the waves of the sea, bent on drinking his enemy's life, bow and arrow raised and red as Death, the prince in the leaf garland was held back by the teacher in the manner that follows.
392.event: Civakan takes up his bow to go and kill Kattiyankaran, and the teacher stops him.

393.reading: The teacher says he asks one great gift; Civakan bids him take whatever he has in mind; the teacher asks that for the span of one year Civakan bear no anger against that man, and the bowman agrees.
393.event: As his fee the teacher asks Civakan to hold back his anger against Kattiyankaran for a year, and Civakan promises.
393.nuance: The request is made as a teacher's due, so Civakan cannot refuse it; it binds the time of the revenge, not its end, and the anger is to be suspended (அழற்சி இன்மை) for a fixed term (யாண்டு நேர் எல்லை).

394.reading: Seeing Civakan's unshaken firmness, like that of tempered steel, a treasure that harsh deeds dare not approach, the teacher, his own disquiet gone and the flaring anger quenched, began to tell what had befallen a certain man.
394.event: The teacher begins the story of 'a certain man', which is his own.
394.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are dense: அமிர்தம் இன்னீர் கவ்விய எஃகின் is read as steel that has drunk its quenching water, and வெவ் வினை வெகுண்டு சாரா as a treasure that harsh deeds do not come near; other construals are possible. The story is told of ஒருவன், and only in 397 does the teacher say it is himself.

395.reading: The teacher tells of Lokamapalan, king of Varanavasi on the silver mountain of the sky, who set his young son on the throne and, having weighed it patiently as a heron waits, took on the guise of the ascetics.
395.event: Lokamapalan, a Vidyadhara king, crowns his son and becomes an ascetic.
395.nuance: பண்ணவர் படிவம் is the outward form of the ascetics of the Jina, so the renunciation is marked as Jain by its dress; the white heron is an image of patient, considered watching, not haste.

396.reading: This man of guileless resolve, who began a great penance so that fierce anger might wane and leave him, was overtaken by sin: wasted by the hunger-fire that roars like an elephant, he gave way in his vow and came into the mansions of this old city.
396.event: During his penance the ascetic is struck by the elephant-fire hunger and comes to the city to be fed.

claims.claim: sin from former deeds can overtake even one who does penance with a guileless mind

396.nuance: The ascetic's penance was undertaken against வெஞ்சினம், the very anger he has just asked Civakan to suspend (393), so his request comes from his own discipline. The verse names no deed as the cause, only that பாவம் வந்து அடைந்தது; the school is Jain as the passage presents it (பண்ணவர் in 395, the people of the Jina's house in 402).

397.reading: Hearing the tale before it was finished, the young man looked up gladly and asked who that man was, long may he live; the teacher said 'I am he', and Civakan, delighted, bade him go on with his words sweet as nectar from the milk sea.
397.event: The teacher reveals that the man of the story is himself, and Civakan asks him to continue.
397.nuance: The structure doubles the scene of 389: each teller first tells a story in the third person and then says to the listener that its subject is the one before him, Civakan in 389, the teacher in 397.

398.reading: The teacher recalls how the boy, to eat the sweet milk-rice cooked from the milk of red cows that graze on flowers, climbed with his companions onto a seat beyond praise on a golden floor spread with golden plates.
398.event: The boy Civakan sits down with his friends to a rich meal in his foster father's house.

399.reading: As he ate the nectar-food served by graceful women, he saw the teacher standing in the entrance, came over and said 'come up', and they served the guest too on a golden dish like the sun over the sea.
399.event: The boy sees the hungry ascetic at the door and invites him to the meal.
399.nuance: It is the child, not the householder, who sees the stranger at the door and calls him in.

400.reading: Pouring handfuls of fragrant ghee and bringing pots of jaggery, the boy kept saying 'serve, serve', till the teacher's sides swelled as if the silver mountain were being poured into the great sea to fill it; by the master's grace, he says, he became one who does the work of the learned.
400.event: Fed without stint at the boy's bidding, the ascetic is cured of his hunger and becomes a teacher.
400.nuance: The hunger is the measure of the cure: what is poured in is a mountain into the sea. அந்தணர் தொழிலன் ஆனேன் turns the cured ascetic into a teacher, so the meal is the cause of Civakan's education. The verse credits the cure to the boy's grace (ஐயன் அது அருளினால்), a child's gift doing what a vow could not.

401.reading: Sunandai of the bee-thronged garland and her husband welcomed and cared for him, and freed from the elephant-fire he stayed on, caught, he tells Civakan, in the net of a youth like the god of love with the sugarcane bow.
401.event: Kantukkatan and Sunandai keep the cured ascetic in their house, and he stays for love of the boy.

402.reading: Your father's house, he says, holds red-gold wealth the earth could not bear and is open to all the people of the four-faced Lord under the Pindi tree; therefore he entered it, and there saw the boy among the women.
402.event: The teacher explains that he came to the merchant's house because it received the Jina's devotees.
402.nuance: பிண்டி நான் முகன் is the Jina seated under the asoka (பிண்டி), and தமர் his followers: the foster home is a Jain household, and its hospitality to ascetics is why the meeting happened. நுந்தை here is Kantukkatan, the foster father.

403.reading: When he saw the boy, the elephant-fire within him shrank like a hooded snake that has seen the antidote; awed, wondering whether this was a god, he heard a resounding sound, as of nectar rising, that would put a war drum to shame.
403.event: At the sight of the boy the ascetic's disease abates and he hears a sound like a drum.
403.nuance: The sound of line 4 is not identified: it may be the boy's voice, or a sign that marks him; read as the teacher's sign that the child was more than human. அதகம் is the antidote that subdues a snake.

404.reading: He tells the young lion, whose garland of pearls rings him like a rainbow about the young crescent, that his words beyond measure and his bright beauty were made by his horoscope.

claims.claim: the birth chart shapes a person's eloquence and beauty

405.reading: The tiger-like bowman, hearing this, says that with penance as mother and the teacher as father he has been created anew, and blesses him; the teacher replies that he will now stand in the true path.
405.event: Civakan calls the teacher his father, and the teacher announces that he will return to the ascetic path.

claims.claim: a teacher who forms one is a father, and his penance a mother

405.nuance: The prince who has just learned that his mother left him in the forest and that he was raised by a foster house now names a third parentage, the teacher's.

406.reading: If one says 'I will leave home without stain and do great penance', the teacher says, the greatly wise speak of no other dharma but bid him take up renunciation; and he stood worshipping the prince's feet.
406.event: The teacher asks Civakan's leave to renounce and bows to him.

claims.claim: when one resolves to leave home for penance, the wise urge only the way of renunciation

406.nuance: Who speaks lines 1 to 3, and who is நல் மணி வண்ணன் அன்னான் in line 4, is not fixed by the verse; it is read as the teacher asking leave and bowing to the prince he has called master (ஐயன், 400), but it could be Civakan giving leave. துறவறம் is set against பிற அறம், which includes the household life the teacher has lived in the merchant's house.

407.reading: Having written into the mind of the lion-like prince, whose fierce anger will not stay in bounds, the policy by which enemies are destroyed, the teacher consoled the merchant's wife and the merchant who dwells among sea-borne wealth.
407.event: Before leaving, the teacher instructs Civakan in the policy of defeating enemies and comforts his foster parents.
407.nuance: The construal that the teacher wrote the policy into Civakan's mind, rather than into his own, is the more natural reading of lines 1 and 2 but not certain.

408.reading: Sunandai, melting inwardly like butter by the fire, her flute-like voice failing, asks whether he will leave the boy alone; he would not stay, and the Vidyadhara king went away to do the penance that wears down old deeds.
408.event: Ignoring Sunandai's plea, the teacher leaves to resume his penance.

claims.claim: penance wears away the deeds of the past

408.nuance: பழவினை பரிய நோற்பான் names the aim of the renewed penance as wearing away (பரிய) old deeds, the Jain account of release; it closes the account begun in 396, where those deeds broke his first penance.

links.note: 387 names the birth star Uttirattathi; 404 makes the horoscope the cause of the prince's eloquence and beauty.
links.teaches: The birth scene's star is not ornament: the teacher reads Civakan's qualities as written at that birth, so the foundling's worth was fixed before his parentage was known.

links.note: The teacher tells Civakan that his enemy still stands and not to lament; the next verse shows the rage this rouses, which the teacher must then restrain.
links.teaches: The consolation that turns grief into thoughts of the enemy produces the very anger the teacher at once has to check, so his own counsel makes the year of restraint necessary.

links.note: The teacher asks Civakan to bear no anger for a year; his own penance had been undertaken so that fierce anger would wane.
links.teaches: The request for restraint is the teacher's own discipline passed to his pupil, asked by one who knows how hard anger is to wear down.

links.note: The teacher binds Civakan to a year without anger toward Kattiyankaran, yet before leaving writes into his mind the policy of destroying enemies.
links.teaches: The ascetic's restraint on his pupil is a postponement of revenge rather than its renunciation: anger is suspended while the means of war are taught.

links.note: Sin overtook the ascetic in his first penance; at the end he goes to resume penance to wear down old deeds.
links.teaches: The teacher's life runs in a circle through Civakan's house: a penance broken by the fruit of past deeds is taken up again, with the wearing away of those deeds now named as its aim.

links.note: The mother left the newborn to aram in the forest; the grown son now says penance was his mother and the teacher his father.
links.teaches: The child commended to dharma by a departing mother is answered, in the son's own words, by a parentage of penance and teaching, as if aram had taken him up through the ascetic.

links.note: Both epics give the elephant-fire hunger and both measure it by mountains poured into the sea: here the silver mountain filling the sea, there the hills the monkeys threw into the ocean.
links.teaches: The Jain and the Buddhist epic share the disease and its image, but the Cintamani cures it with a child's meal in a Jain household while the Manimekalai cures it with the bowl of a renunciant, so each makes its own kind of giver the remedy.

links.note: Manimekalai traces Kayasandikai's elephant-fire to a named act, crushing an ascetic's fruit, and his curse; the Cintamani says only that sin came upon the ascetic in his penance.
links.teaches: Set beside the Manimekalai's exact chain of act, curse and term, the Cintamani's unnamed sin shows karma striking even a guileless penitent with no deed in this life to explain it.

links.note: The couplet ranks the strength of those who relieve hunger above that of those who endure it; the ascetic's endurance fails and a child's feeding saves him.
links.teaches: The epic stages the couplet's ranking as one scene: the ascetic's strength to bear hunger breaks, and the boy's strength to relieve it restores him and gives Civakan his teacher.

gains.a: the meal gains a moral rank: the boy's act stands above the ascetic's vow, not merely beside it
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which the endurer is himself rescued by the reliever, so the ranking is shown to be needed, not only stated

links.note: The couplet defines penance as bearing the pain that comes; the ascetic's penance gives way under the hunger-fire and he goes to the city to eat.
links.teaches: The epic marks a limit to the couplet's definition: there are pains, sent by past deeds, that a penitent cannot bear, and his penance has to be suspended and later resumed.

gains.a: the ascetic's lapse is measured against a standard, so his leaving the vow reads as failure under pain rather than mere misfortune
gains.b: the definition gains a case where the pain that comes is beyond bearing, raising what penance does then

links.note: The couplet bids one forget anger at anyone at all; the teacher asks Civakan to hold his anger against one man for one year only.
links.teaches: Against the couplet's unlimited forgetting of anger, the epic's ascetic sets a term to restraint, so a teacher who renounced anger for himself still leaves a prince's just anger intact for its time.

gains.a: the request is seen to be partial: it is a delay with an end, not the forgetting the ethics books ask
gains.b: the couplet's 'at anyone at all' is tested by the case of a usurper who killed one's father, where even an ascetic does not ask for it

links.note: The couplet asks what one gains by leaving a household life lived in dharma; the epic holds that once a man resolves to leave home for penance, the wise speak of no other dharma.
links.teaches: The two meet on a condition the couplet leaves out: the Kural weighs the householder's path before the choice, while the epic speaks of one who has already resolved, for whom the household dharma is no longer an option.

gains.a: the epic's claim is placed against the strongest defence of the household, so its scope (one who has resolved) becomes visible
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question gains an answer from a man who has lived both lives, an ascetic who spent years in a merchant's house and returns to penance

links.note: The couplet says the fruit of hospitality is as great as the guest's worth; the merchant's house that fed a hungry stranger gained a Vidyadhara king as the teacher of its son.
links.teaches: The epic shows the couplet's measure working through time: the guest's worth was hidden when he came hungry to the door, and the fruit appeared only as the education of the boy who fed him.

gains.a: the long stay of the cured ascetic is read as the return on a gift, which the verse itself leaves implicit
gains.b: the couplet's measure by the guest's worth gains a case where that worth was unknown to the host, so hospitality cannot be rationed by it

links.note: Tirumular has grace come as the guru and end the soul's own doing; in the Cintamani the guru is himself a karma-bound ascetic who goes off to wear down his old deeds by his own penance.
links.teaches: The two texts set the guru on opposite sides of karma: for Tirumular the guru is the descent of grace that ends one's deeds, while the Cintamani's teacher, having formed his pupil, must still work off his own past by effort.

gains.a: the teacher's departure is seen as a doctrinal statement, release by one's own penance with no grace to end it
gains.b: the Saiva verse's guru as grace gains a clear contrast, a guru who needs release himself, which sharpens what 'guru as grace' claims

source_issues: Verses 386 to 393 and 395 to 408 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 387 line 3 prints தோன்றி னானே with a space inside the word.
Verse 394 lines 1 and 2 (வெவ் வினை வெகுண்டு சாரா விழுநிதி அமிர்தம் இன்னீர் கவ்விய எஃகின்) are obscure as printed.
Verse 403 line 4 (மொய் குரல் முரசம் நாணும் தழங்கு குரல்) does not say whose voice or what sound is meant.
Verse 406 does not mark who speaks lines 1 to 3 or whom நல் மணி வண்ணன் அன்னான் names.
